Aggregate

AG-ruh-gayt — ends like 'gate'; picture herding scattered data through one gate into a single flock. · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To aggregate is to gather separate items and combine them into a single whole.

The website aggregates headlines from dozens of newspapers into a single feed.

Worked Example

A researcher collects test scores from fifty different schools. She merges them all into one master spreadsheet. Only then can she study the overall pattern across the whole state.

Combining many separate pieces into one unified collection is to aggregate them. Unlike 'collect,' which just means gathering things up, aggregating merges them into a single whole you can work with.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

combine: to join separate things together

compile: to gather items into one collection where each stays separate and whole; aggregate fuses them into a single combined total

pool: to put resources into one shared collection

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

separate: to divide into parts

scatter: to spread widely apart

Where it sits · how completely the parts merge — gather → aggregate → consolidate

gather vs. aggregate: To gather is weaker than to aggregate — gathering just brings things near each other, while aggregating fuses them into one usable whole.

consolidate vs. aggregate: To consolidate is stronger than to aggregate: aggregating combines items into a whole, but consolidating merges them so completely that the separate parts disappear.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — ag- (ad-)

prefix — ag- (ad-): to, toward (Latin)

root — greg-

root — greg-: flock, herd (Latin)

suffix — -ate

suffix — -ate: to make or do (verb-forming) (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: Latin ad- (toward) plus grex (flock) means 'to drive toward the flock.' To aggregate is to herd scattered members together into one group.

Use the root in a new word: congregate
